scenes.narration: Six months into any calendar year, the gap between loud January resolutions and quiet behavioral architecture becomes impossible to ignore. Willpower-driven sprints fizzle out by mid-February, leaving behind unused subscriptions and half-finished notebooks. Meanwhile, someone protecting just five calm morning hours a week across twenty-six consecutive weeks has quietly banked one hundred and thirty hours of deep asset creation alongside automated monthly savings. To make your next twenty-six weeks compound even cleaner than your last, we are locking five classic economic and psychological breakthroughs into one repeatable half-year operating system.

scenes.tag: CHAPTER 2 • COASE & THE LEAN SOLO STUDIO
scenes.headline: Why Falling Transaction Costs Favor One-Person Builders
scenes.left_body: High external coordination costs -> giant bureaucracy & meeting tax
scenes.right_body: Code + templates + AI collapse friction -> 1 owner ships globally
scenes.narration: Layer One begins with Nobel economist Ronald Coase and his landmark 1937 Economica paper, 'The Nature of the Firm.' Coase asked a foundational question: if markets are efficient, why do giant companies with layers of middle managers exist at all? His answer was transaction costs, the friction of negotiating, coordinating, and verifying every step across outsiders. Today, Python scripts, cloud distribution, and modern AI pipelines collapse those production costs near zero while big firms drown in internal status meetings. Keeping your operation to one clear owner plus deterministic software lets five weekly hours produce output that once required a whole department.
scenes.source: Ronald H. Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm', Economica (1937)

scenes.headline: Pre-Committing Future Cashflow Before Lifestyle Creep
scenes.stat_label: SAVE MORE TOMORROW TRIPLED RETIREMENT SAVING RATES
scenes.stat_subtext: 3.5% -> 13.6% savings rate across 4 pay raises • Zero take-home pain
scenes.narration: Layer Two funds your personal runway without austerity, drawing on Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's 2004 Journal of Political Economy study, 'Save More Tomorrow.' Instead of asking workers to slash today's grocery budget, Thaler and Benartzi had employees pre-commit a slice of future pay raises directly into investments before the extra money ever hit checking. Across four raises, average savings rates climbed from three-point-five percent to thirteen-point-six percent. Apply the exact ratchet at your half-year review: route half of every salary bump, bonus, or new digital asset dollar straight into broad index funds.
scenes.source: Thaler & Benartzi, 'Save More Tomorrow', Journal of Political Economy (2004)

scenes.headline: Protecting Creation Blocks From Weekday Fatigue
scenes.stat_label: FIXED IF-THEN CUES BYPASS DAILY NEGOTIATION
bullets: Peter Gollwitzer (1999): bind goal intentions to exact time & place
Block A: Saturday 7:00-9:30 AM -> research & write flagship asset
Block B: Sunday 7:00-9:30 AM -> render, verify & schedule week
scenes.narration: Layer Three converts good creative intentions into unbroken shipping using psychologist Peter Gollwitzer's 1999 research on Implementation Intentions. Never leave your five weekly asset hours floating inside weekday evenings when your cognitive fuel is already spent by your day job. Anchor them to unbreakable If-Then cues before the world wakes up. For example: 'If it is seven AM Saturday at my clear desk, then my phone stays in the kitchen while I write one flagship essay for two and a half hours. If it is seven AM Sunday, then I render, verify, and schedule the week's four finished assets before breakfast.'
scenes.source: Peter M. Gollwitzer, 'Implementation Intentions', American Psychologist (1999)

scenes.headline: Subtracting Six Months of Barnacles Before Q3
scenes.left_body: Adams (2021): piling Q3 goals onto Q1 clutter -> autumn burnout
scenes.right_body: Drucker (1964): exit every commitment you wouldn't enter fresh today
scenes.narration: Even a clean studio accumulates barnacles across twenty-six weeks, which is why Layer Four combines Gabrielle Adams's 2021 Nature research on subtraction with Peter Drucker's 1964 abandonment rule. Adams and her co-authors proved our brains instinctively add new tasks when reviewing progress instead of deleting friction. Counter that bias before Quarter Three starts by running Drucker's question across every recurring expense, software tool, content format, and obligation: 'If I were not already in this today, knowing what I now know, would I enter it now?' Every honest 'no' gets retired this week so your best energy stays unsplit.
scenes.source: Adams et al., Nature (2021); Peter F. Drucker, Managing for Results (1964)

scenes.headline: Execute Your 60-Minute Half-Year Review Today
scenes.stat_label: AUTOMATE • RATCHET • LOCK 5 HOURS • PRUNE 3 DRAINS
bullets: 1. Coase Filter: automate or cut 1 manual bottleneck in your workflow
2. Thaler Ratchet: raise automatic payday investing by +1% to +2%
3. Gollwitzer + Drucker: lock 5 weekend morning hours & exit 3 dead drains
scenes.narration: Block sixty quiet minutes this weekend and execute all four steps in order. Step One, the Coase Filter: inspect your production workflow and automate or eliminate one repetitive manual step so your studio stays friction-free. Step Two, the Save More Tomorrow Ratchet: nudge your automatic payday investment transfer up by one or two percent, and pre-assign half of any second-half windfalls to investments. Step Three, the Gollwitzer Lock: put your Saturday and Sunday morning If-Then blocks onto the calendar for the next twenty-six weeks. Step Four, the Drucker-Adams Prune: cancel three dead bills or commitments tonight, and enter the second half lighter, wealthier, and compounding.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin 6-Month OS: Coase (1937), Thaler (2004), Gollwitzer (1999), Adams (2021), Drucker (1964)
